lead: Choosing a material means matching what the part must do to the numbers a material offers. A tie that must not stretch permanently needs yield strength, a lever that must not bend out of line needs stiffness, a bush that slides needs hardness, and a hook that may be jerked needs toughness. No single number decides: the designer screens candidates on the properties the part needs, sizes the part in each, and then compares mass and cost. The same reasoning picks mild steel for a fan bracket, cast iron for a lathe bed and aluminium alloy for a bicycle crank.
prereq: You need the factors from the design process.

blocks.text: A tensile test, pulling a bar until it breaks, gives most of them.

items: Yield strength Syt (MPa): the stress at which permanent deformation starts. A ductile part is designed against it.
Ultimate tensile strength Sut (MPa): the highest stress the bar carries. A brittle part, which breaks without yielding, is designed against it.

Modulus of elasticity E (GPa): stress divided by strain in the elastic range. It sets stiffness, not strength. All steels have E of about 200 to 210 GPa, so heat treatment that triples the strength leaves the deflection unchanged.
Ductility: the percentage elongation at fracture. Above about 5 % the material is called ductile (mild steel, about 20 to 25 %); below it, brittle (grey cast iron, under 1 %).
Toughness (J): the energy absorbed up to fracture, the area under the whole stress-strain curve; needed for shock loads. Resilience is the energy stored elastically, Syt²/(2E) per unit volume.
Hardness (Brinell HB, Vickers HV, Rockwell): resistance to indentation, a guide to wear resistance.
Fatigue strength for repeated loads and creep strength for long service at high temperature; see failure theories and fatigue design.

blocks.text: Beside these the designer checks density ρ (kg/m³) for mass, corrosion resistance, machinability, weldability, castability and cost (₹/kg).

blocks.text: Indian standards name steels by composition. In 40C8 the 40 means 0.40 % carbon (in hundredths of a per cent) and the 8 means about 0.8 % manganese (ten times the manganese content); an alloy steel such as 40Cr4 has 0.40 % carbon and about 1 % chromium. Grey cast iron FG 200 has a minimum tensile strength of 200 MPa, and spheroidal graphite iron SG 500/7 has 500 MPa with 7 % elongation. Look up the property values for a grade in your design data book; the numbers in this chapter are typical values for teaching.

items: Write the load, the failure mode (yield, fracture, wear, deflection), the environment and the number to be made.
Screen out materials that cannot work: a brittle material for a shock-loaded hook, plain steel in sea water without a coating.
Size the part in each remaining material, once for strength and once for stiffness; the larger section governs.
Compare the sized parts on mass and cost, then on making and finishing.

blocks.text: A light tie of given strength needs the largest S<sub>yt</sub>/ρ (specific strength); one of given stiffness needs the largest E/ρ (specific stiffness). Steel and aluminium have almost the same E/ρ (25.5 and 25.6 GPa per tonne/m³), so a stiffness-limited tie is no lighter in aluminium. Only a few syllabi teach these material indices.

The weighted-point method scores each candidate on each property out of 100: for a larger-is-better property, 100 × value/best value; for cost, 100 × lowest cost/its cost. Each score is multiplied by a weight (the weights add up to 1) and the products are summed. The highest total wins, provided no single property failed the screen.

examples.question: A tie rod 500 mm long carries a steady pull of 20 kN. It must have a factor of safety of 2 on yield and must not stretch more than 0.6 mm. Three materials are offered: mild steel (S<sub>yt</sub> = 250 MPa, E = 200 GPa, ρ = 7850 kg/m³, ₹60/kg), aluminium alloy 6061-T6 (276 MPa, 69 GPa, 2700 kg/m³, ₹300/kg) and a quenched and tempered alloy steel (650 MPa, 200 GPa, 7850 kg/m³, ₹120/kg). Size the rod in each material, and choose the material for the lowest mass and for the lowest cost.
steps: Strength: the allowable stress is S<sub>yt</sub>/2, so the area needed is A = 2F/S<sub>yt</sub>. With F = 20,000 N: mild steel 40,000/250 = 160.0 mm²; aluminium 40,000/276 = 144.9 mm²; alloy steel 40,000/650 = 61.5 mm².
Governing area (the larger of the two): mild steel 160.0 mm² (strength); aluminium 241.5 mm² (stiffness); alloy steel 83.3 mm² (stiffness).
Mass m = ρAL with A in m² and L = 0.5 m. Mild steel: 7850 × 160.0 × 10⁻⁶ × 0.5 = 0.628 kg. Aluminium: 2700 × 241.5 × 10⁻⁶ × 0.5 = 0.326 kg. Alloy steel: 7850 × 83.3 × 10⁻⁶ × 0.5 = 0.327 kg.
Cost: mild steel 0.628 × 60 = ₹37.7; aluminium 0.326 × 300 = ₹97.8; alloy steel 0.327 × 120 = ₹39.2.
Check: at its strength size of 144.9 mm², aluminium would stretch 20,000 × 500/(144.9 × 69,000) = 1.00 mm, which is why stiffness governs there; mild steel at 160 mm² stretches only 0.31 mm.
examples.answer: Mild steel needs 160 mm² (0.628 kg, ₹37.7), aluminium 241.5 mm² (0.326 kg, ₹97.8) and alloy steel 83.3 mm² (0.327 kg, ₹39.2). Aluminium is lightest by only 1 g; alloy steel is almost as light at about a third of its cost, so alloy steel is the sensible choice, with mild steel if mass does not matter.

examples.question: A bracket for a coastal pump house can be mild steel, aluminium alloy 6061-T6 or stainless steel 304. Data: yield strength 250, 276 and 215 MPa; E 200, 69 and 193 GPa; cost ₹60, ₹300 and ₹250 per kg; corrosion rating out of 5: 1, 4 and 5. Weights: strength 0.25, stiffness 0.15, cost 0.35, corrosion 0.25. Rank the materials by the weighted-point method.
steps: Scaled strength (best 276): mild steel 100 × 250/276 = 90.6; aluminium 100; stainless 100 × 215/276 = 77.9.
examples.answer: Mild steel 77.6, stainless 67.3, aluminium 57.2. Mild steel wins on cost, but only if a protective coating (galvanising or paint) is specified for the salt air; if coating is not allowed, the corrosion screen removes it and stainless steel is chosen.

traps: Raising strength to cut deflection. Heat treatment raises S<sub>yt</sub> but not E, so a stiffness-limited steel part does not get stiffer.
Designing a ductile part on S<sub>ut</sub>, or a brittle part on a yield strength it does not have. Grey cast iron has no clear yield point.
Confusing hardness with toughness. A hardened file is hard but brittle; a mild steel hook is soft but tough.
Comparing materials by strength alone. Size the part in each, then compare mass and cost, as in the tie-rod example.
Reading 40C8 as 40 % carbon. It is 0.40 % carbon and about 0.8 % manganese.

quiz.q: Define yield strength, ultimate tensile strength and modulus of elasticity.
quiz.a: Yield strength: stress at which permanent deformation starts. Ultimate tensile strength: the highest stress in a tensile test. Modulus of elasticity: stress/strain in the elastic range; it measures stiffness.

quiz.q: What do the designations 40C8 and FG 200 mean?
quiz.a: 40C8: plain carbon steel with 0.40 % carbon and about 0.8 % manganese. FG 200: grey cast iron with a minimum tensile strength of 200 MPa.

Toughness is the energy absorbed up to fracture (area under the whole stress-strain curve). Resilience is the energy stored elastically up to yield, S<sub>yt</sub>²/(2E) per unit volume, and is recovered on unloading.

quiz.q: Find the modulus of resilience of mild steel with S<sub>yt</sub> = 250 MPa and E = 200 GPa.
In the tie-rod example aluminium needed 241.5 mm² but only 144.9 mm² for strength. Explain why, and say when aluminium would win clearly.
quiz.a: Its E is about a third of steel's, so the stretch limit needs a larger area; stiffness governs. Aluminium wins clearly when strength governs and mass matters, because its S<sub>yt</sub>/ρ is about three times that of mild steel.

beyond: Materials engineers choose from tens of thousands of grades with selection software such as Ansys Granta Selector, which plots property charts (E against ρ, strength against cost) and applies material indices automatically. Sustainability now enters the choice: embodied energy and carbon per kilogram, and whether the part can be recycled. Search next for Ashby material selection charts, material indices and life-cycle assessment.

figure.caption: The tie rod of the first worked example sized in each material: the word in brackets is the check that set its area. Aluminium is lighter than alloy steel by only a gram, because stiffness, not strength, governs both, but it costs two and a half times as much.
